  chunk_output_type: console

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  message  = FALSE,
  warning  = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 7,
  fig.height = 2.8,
  fig.retina = 2,
  dpi = 110,
  # The plots require ggplot2 (a Suggests dependency); skip evaluation if absent.
  eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

`energyRt` ships `autoplot()` methods (and, where natural, matching `plot()`
methods) for most of its building-block classes. They turn an object into a
`ggplot`, so the result can be themed and extended with `+` layers like any other
ggplot.

| Class | What the plot shows |
|-------|---------------------|
| `calendar` | the sub-annual time structure (stacked timeframe rows) |
| `horizon` | the planning intervals / milestone years |
| `commodity` | emission factors (`@emis`) — one or several commodities |
| `supply`, `demand`, `import`, `export` | level parameters over years (given data + interpolation) |
| `weather` | a sub-annual capacity/availability factor (heatmap, line or area) |

```{r setup}
library(energyRt)
library(ggplot2)   # provides the autoplot() generic
```

# Calendars

The example `calendars` dataset holds a few ready-made `calendar` objects.

```{r}
data("calendars", package = "energyRt")
names(calendars)
```

`autoplot()` returns each timeframe as a row of rectangles sized by each
timeslice's share of the year; `plot()` draws the same figure:

```{r cal-basic, fig.height = 2.2}
autoplot(calendars$s4_hp3)
```

## Coloring

For `fill = "order"` (the default) the `color_pattern` controls the gradient.
`"within"` (default) colours each level over **its own** timeslices — so an hourly
row shows a full `h00`→`h23` cycle repeating every day, while `"global"` colours
by absolute chronology across the whole year.

```{r cal-color, fig.height = 2.6}
autoplot(calendars$d365_h24)                          # within (default)
autoplot(calendars$d365_h24, color_pattern = "global")
```

Other fill metrics are the timeslice `"share"` and `"weight"`:

```{r cal-share, fig.height = 2.2}
autoplot(calendars$s4_hp3, fill = "share")
```

## Labels

Each cell is labelled by its member name (`labels = "name"`, the default,
e.g. `h00`…`h23`) or by the full timeslice path (`labels = "timeslice"`,
e.g. `d001_h00`); `labels = FALSE` draws none. Label text contrasts with the
fill automatically, and rows with more cells than `max_labels` stay unlabelled.

```{r cal-labels, fig.height = 2.6}
autoplot(calendars$s4_hp3, labels = "timeslice")
```

## Subset view

A reduced calendar can be shown against a full reference calendar: pass the full
one as `reference`. The timeslices present in the subset are filled; the rest are
left empty.

```{r cal-subset, fig.height = 2.4}
autoplot(calendars$d365_h24_1dpm,
         reference = calendars$d365_h24)
```

## Styling

`border` outlines the rectangles (off by default so dense rows read as a smooth
gradient) and `palette` picks the viridis option; and because the result is a
ggplot you can keep customizing it:

```{r cal-style, fig.height = 2.2}
autoplot(calendars$s4_hp3, palette = "magma", border = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Four seasons, day/night") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Heatmaps

`autoplot()` lays every timeslice out in one row per timeframe. When a value is
indexed by a *two-dimensional* calendar — day-of-year × hour, month × hour — a
**heatmap** reads more naturally: `gg_heatmap()` puts the finest timeframe on
`y`, the next on `x`, and any coarser levels into facets. The layout is taken
from the calendar, which you pass as `calendar =` -- either a calendar object or
the name of one, such as `"d365_h24"`.

Here is a synthetic hourly load profile on the `d365_h24` calendar (a daily cycle
plus a seasonal swing). The diurnal band and the winter/summer contrast are
immediately visible:

```{r hm-day, fig.height = 2.6}
calendar_d365h24 <- calendars$d365_h24
timetable <- calendar_d365h24@timetable
hour <- timescales::tsl2hour(timetable$timeslice, calendar_d365h24@name)
yday <- timescales::tsl2yday(timetable$timeslice, calendar_d365h24@name)
prof <- data.frame(
  timeslice = timetable$timeslice,
  load = 50 + 30 * sin(2 * pi * (hour - 6) / 24) +
              15 * cos(2 * pi * yday / 365))

# x = YDAY, y = HOUR
gg_heatmap(prof, calendar = calendar_d365h24, value = "load")
```

Facet a day-of-year format by `"month"` to get one day-of-month × hour panel per
month:

```{r hm-month, fig.height = 4.5}
# 12 panels
gg_heatmap(prof, calendar = calendar_d365h24, value = "load",
             facet = "month")
```

`palette` selects the viridis option and `name` labels the colour bar, exactly as
for `autoplot()`.

## From model objects

Any timeslice-indexed model data lays out the same way. Here **electricity demand**
and a **solar capacity factor** from the packaged TOPIA kit, on its hourly
calendar (`d365_h24`): pull the object with `getObject()`, take one region
(and, for demand, one year), and pass the `timeslice` + value columns to
`gg_heatmap()`. The `name` argument carries the value's unit onto the colour
bar. A graded resource ships one series per grade, so the solar object is cut
to one mounting as well as one region -- two series on one timeslice have
nothing to lay out.

```{r hm-demand, fig.height = 2.6}
repo <- topia$modules$electricity$repo

DEM <- getObject(repo, name = "DEM_ELC", drop = TRUE)
dem <- subset(as.data.frame(DEM@demand), region == "R02" & year == 2025)
gg_heatmap(dem[, c("timeslice", "demand")], calendar = calendar_d365h24,
             value = "demand", name = "GWh", facet = "month")
```

```{r hm-weather, fig.height = 2.6}
WSOL <- getObject(repo, name = "WSOL", drop = TRUE)
wsol <- subset(as.data.frame(WSOL@weather), region == "R02" & cluster == "FL")
gg_heatmap(wsol[, c("timeslice", "wval")], calendar = calendar_d365h24,
             value = "wval", name = "capacity factor", facet = "month")
```

The weather heatmap is exactly what `autoplot()` draws for a `weather` object
directly — with line and area variants too (see *Weather* below).

# Horizons

`horizon` objects draw the modelled intervals over milestone years:

```{r hor, fig.height = 2.4}
data("horizons", package = "energyRt")
autoplot(horizons$Y2020_2060_by_5)
```

# Commodities

For a `commodity`, `autoplot()` shows its emission factors (`@emis`). Passing
several commodities compares their emission intensities side by side.

```{r comm}
COA <- newCommodity("COA", desc = "Coal",
                    emis = data.frame(comm = "CO2", unit = "kt/GWh", emis = 0.33))
OIL <- newCommodity("OIL", emis = data.frame(comm = "CO2", unit = "kt/GWh", emis = 0.25))
GAS <- newCommodity("GAS", emis = data.frame(comm = "CO2", unit = "kt/GWh", emis = 0.18))

autoplot(COA)                 # a single commodity
autoplot(COA, OIL, GAS)       # comparison
```

# Supply, demand, import, export

These process objects are plotted by year: the **points** are the given data and
the **lines** are the interpolation (both extracted with `getData()`). Level
parameters are faceted by their base name so bounds and prices/costs keep
separate y-scales.

```{r sup, fig.height = 3}
SUP_COA <- newSupply(
  name = "SUP_COA", commodity = "COA", unit = "PJ", region = "R1",
  supply = data.frame(
    region = "R1", timeslice = "ANNUAL",
    year   = c(2020, 2040, 2020, 2020),
    ava.up = c(100,  200,  NA,   NA),
    ava.lo = c(NA,   NA,   10,   NA),
    cost   = c(NA,   NA,   NA,   30)))
autoplot(SUP_COA)
```

A single given value (or none) is drawn as a flat dashed line showing the
interpolation direction. Pass `year` to interpolate over a specific horizon
(constant extrapolation beyond the given years), `interpolate = FALSE` to
show only the given data, and `show_defaults = TRUE` to also draw the
model's default values for parameters the object leaves unset:

```{r sup-years, fig.height = 3}
autoplot(SUP_COA, year = 2020:2050)
autoplot(SUP_COA, show_defaults = TRUE)
```

Demand, import and export follow the same pattern:

```{r dem, fig.height = 2.6}
DEM_ELC <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC", commodity = "ELC", unit = "GWh",
  demand = data.frame(region = "R1", timeslice = "ANNUAL",
                   year = c(2020, 2030, 2050), demand = c(100, 150, 300)))
autoplot(DEM_ELC)
```

```{r imp, fig.height = 3}
IMP_GAS <- newImport(
  name = "IMP_GAS", commodity = "GAS",
  import = data.frame(region = "R1", timeslice = "ANNUAL",
                   year = c(2020, 2050), imp.up = c(50, 80), price = c(5, 9)))
autoplot(IMP_GAS)
```

# Weather

`weather` objects hold a sub-annual factor — a capacity / availability factor —
per region and timeslice. `autoplot()` offers three views via `type =`: a calendar
**heatmap** (the default), and diurnal **line** / **area** charts. Because the
timeslice layout (here season × hour) can't be inferred from the timeslice names alone,
pass the model's `calendar`; the value's unit (`getUnit()`, or `"capacity factor"`
when unset) labels the value axis — the fill legend for the heatmap, the y-axis
for line/area.

```{r wea, fig.height = 3}
WSOL <- getObject(topia$modules$electricity$repo,
                  name = "WSOL", drop = TRUE)

# heatmap (default), faceted by region
autoplot(WSOL, calendar = calendar_d365h24)
```

The **line** view reads the diurnal shape directly — one line per season, the
capacity factor on the y-axis:

```{r wea-line, fig.height = 3}
autoplot(WSOL, style = "line", calendar = calendar_d365h24)
autoplot(WSOL, style = "area", calendar = calendar_d365h24)   # or filled areas
```

# Notes

* Every method returns a `ggplot`, so `+ theme_*()`, `+ labs()`, `+ scale_*()`
  etc. all work.
* `plot()` is available for `calendar` and `horizon`: it draws the `autoplot()`
  figure and returns it invisibly.
* `autoplot()` also works on the result of `levcost()` (levelized cost) — see
  `?levcost` — but that requires solving a small model, so it is not shown here.
* See `?autoplot.calendar`, `?autoplot.commodity`, `?autoplot.supply`, and
  `?plot_weather` for the full list of arguments.
